nodes.name: Lempert-Szőke curvature condition for entire tubes
nodes.statement: Lempert and Sz\H{o}ke \cite{ls} have shown that a necessary condition for the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire is that the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative.
assumptions: the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire
conclusions: the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative

nodes.name: Szőke's classification of entire tubes for metrics of revolution on $S^2$
nodes.statement: Sz\H{o}ke has shown that there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes, whereas many of these manifolds have strictly positive curvature.
conclusions: there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes

nodes.name: Aguilar's higher order conditions for entire tubes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $M$ of two dimensions, Aguilar \cite{a2} has found an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire.
conclusions: an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire

nodes.name: Effective finiteness of Aguilar's conditions
nodes.statement: In particular, it is not known whether the conditions are effectively finite, i.e., are redundant after a certain degree.

nodes.name: Szőke: bi-invariant metrics have entire tubes
nodes.statement: If the metric $g$ is bi-invariant on $G$, then Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s} has shown that the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$.
conclusions: the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$

nodes.name: Left-invariant metrics with negative scalar curvature have no entire tube
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is well-known that some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$, which shows they cannot have entire tubes, by Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke's condition.
conclusions: some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$, which shows they cannot have entire tubes

nodes.name: Arnol'd: geodesic flow of a left-invariant metric is the free rigid body
nodes.statement: It is a well-known observation of Arnol'd that the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass (see \cite{via}, Appendix 2, for example).
also_stated_at: We will use, from Arnold \cite{via}, that the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group is equivalent to the rotation of a rigid body with frame in $G$ about its center of mass.
assumptions: a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group
conclusions: the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass

nodes.name: Entire tube of a homogeneous space is $G_{\mathbb{C}}/H_{\mathbb{C}}$

nodes.name: Adapted complex structure
nodes.statement: An {\em adapted complex structure} on $T^RM := \{v \in TM \, | \, |v| < R\}$ is a complex structure for which the leaves of the Riemann foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $TM \setminus 0_M$ are complex submanifolds.

nodes.name: Grauert tube

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lemma:action}, we know that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$. We will prove that it acts locally transitively at every point $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$. Assuming this for the moment, this proves that all orbits of $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are open, and since $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is connected, this proves that the mapping $A_v: G_{\mathbb{C}} \ni h \to h\cdot v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, for any fixed $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, is surjective. Since $G_{\mathbb{C}}, M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are of the same complex dimension, and the map $A_v$ is $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a regular value of $A_v$, and hence, $A_v$ is a topological covering. If $v \in M$, the covering $A_v: G \to M$ is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions $G \subset G_{\mathbb{C}}, M \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are homotopy equivalences, the covering $A_v$ has degree 1 over all of $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and therefore $A_v$ is a global biholomorphism. \vskip 2mm \vskip 2mm To show that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that \[ DA_{v}: T^{1,0}_{I} G_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} \to T_v^{1,0} M_{\mathbb{C}} \] is an isomorphism. This, in turn is equivalent to showing that, for a basis $\xi_1, \xi_2,\ldots, \xi_n$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\mathbb{R}$, the complex fields $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2, \ldots, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n$ are a basis for $T^{1,0}M_{\mathbb{C}}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ at $v$. Define $\mathcal{P} = \{ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1 \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n = 0\}$. We wish to show $\mathcal{P}$ is empty. \vskip 2mm Assume it is not empty. Then $\mathcal{P}$ is a $G_{\mathbb{C}}$-invariant divisor on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and $\mathcal{P} \cap M = \emptyset$. Consider the plurisubharmonic function $u$ restricted to $\mathcal{P}$. Since $u$ is non-negative and proper when restricted to $\mathcal{P}$, it achieves a global minimum at some $v \in \mathcal{P}$. The map $A_v$ restricted to $G$ gives an embedding of $G$ into $\mathcal{P} \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ where it is a $CR$-submanifold of real dimension $n$. Note that the function $u$ is constant on $S_v := A_v(G)$. Since $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathcal{P} < n$, $S_v$ cannot be a totally real submanifold in $\mathcal{P}$. Hence its complex tangent space is positive dimensional at every point. Its Levi-form cannot be trivial, since otherwise the leaves of the Levi foliation of $S_v$ would give positive-dimensional complex submanifolds in the level set $\{u = u(v)\}$, which is strictly pseudoconvex, by the tube construction. By a classical construction in complex analysis (local Bishop disks), there exists a continuous mapping $F: \bar{\triangle} \to U \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$, where $U$ is a small polydisk neighborhood of $v$, and with $F|_{\triangle}$ holomorphic and non-constant, and $F(\partial \triangle) \subset S_v$. Thus $u\circ F|_{\partial\triangle} \equiv u(v)$. Therefore, $F(\triangle) \subset \mathcal{P} \cap U$, since $\mathcal{P} \cap U$ is closed and analytic in $U$, which gives us that $u\circ F(z) \geq u(v),$ for all $z \in \triangle$. By the maximum principle, $u\circ F$ is constant on $\triangle$, contradicting, again, the strict pseudoconvexity of $S_v$.

nodes.name: Conjugation on $G=\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement: To fix ideas, if $G = \mathbb{R}$ (at this point we do not need to assume our group $G$ is compact) with the Euclidean metric and unit tangent vector $\frac{d}{dx}$, so that $\mathfrak{g} \cong \mathbb{R} \frac{d}{dx} $, then $G_{\mathbb{C}}\cong \mathbb{C}$ with coordinate $z = x+iy$, and $\widetilde{(\frac{d}{dx})}^{1,0} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ on $\mathbb{C}$. nodes.name: Distinct eigenvalues: complexified geodesics are not entire
nodes.statement: Now the map $v: \mathbb{C} \to C_{a,b} \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ associated to a complexified geodesic with initial conditions $a = E(\gamma(0)), b = M(\gamma(0)),$ must actually map into the affine piece $C^{{aff}}_{a,b} = C_{a,b} \cap \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} = C_{a,b} \setminus C_{a,b} \cap \{w = 0\}$. But this last intersection is non-empty and a holomorphic map of $\mathbb{C}$ to $C^{aff}_{a,b}$ must factor through the universal covering $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to C_{a,b}$, but must omit the infinite set $\pi^{-1}(C_{a,b} \cap\{w = 0\})$. Thus, the map $c$ must be constant, by Picard's theorem. In real terms, this means that the real geodesic satisfies \[ \dot{\gamma} \equiv \xi \in \mathfrak{g}, \] If we assume, without loss of generality, that $\gamma(0) = e \in G,$ this means that $\gamma(s)$ is the 1-parameter subgroup $\exp(s \xi)$ of $G$. Now this conclusion holds true for all initial conditions $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_0$ in a dense open set of $\mathfrak{g} = T_0G.$ By continuity of solution of ODEs, this must hold true for all geodesics passing through 0, and hence, by left translation, for all geodesics. However, it is well-known that any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round (see e.g. \cite{o}, ch. 11, Proposition 9). This would contradict our assumption that the $\lambda_i$ are all distinct.

nodes.statement: To be specific, we set $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, the other case being similar. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement: This is an immediate consequence of a result of Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s2} (cf also \cite{a1}). The metric (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) has an isometry group $G \times S^1$ where the factor $S^1$ acts by right multiplication on $G$ by the 1-parameter subgroup $e^{t\, \xi_3}$ on the right, i.e., by $R_{e^{t\, \xi_3}}$, periodic of period $2\pi$, and the factor $G$ acts by left multiplication $L_g$ on $G$. Consider the manifold $G \times S^1$, where $G$ is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda_1= 1$, and the $S^1$ factor is given the metric $\mu d\theta^2,$ where $d\theta^2$ is the invariant metric of length $2\pi$ on $S^1$ and $\mu$ is a real constant $> 0$. So $G\times S^1$ has the metric $g_{\mu}$ defined by \begin{equation} g_{\mu} = g_I \oplus \mu \, d\theta^2. \end{equation} Consider the quotient manifold of $G\times S^1$ by the action of $S^1 = \{e^{i t}\}$ on $G\times S^1$ given by $e^{i t} \cdot (g, e^{i \theta}) = (g\cdot e^{2 t\, \xi_3}, e^{i(\theta + t)}).$ Then it is easy to see that the quotient manifold $G\times S^1/\sim$ is diffeomorphic to $G$. Let $\bar{g}_{\mu}$ be the Riemannian submersion metric from (\ref{eqn:gmu}). By construction, this metric is invariant under left translation by $G$ and by right translation by $e^{- t \, \xi_3}$. Consequently, it is one of the left invariant metrics on $G$ with an extra isometric action from the right. It is an easy calculation to see which ones arise in this manner. Let \begin{equation} A = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & \lambda \end{array}\right). \end{equation} Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that $g_A(\xi_1, \xi_1) = g_A(\xi_2, \xi_2) = \frac14,$ and $g_A(\xi_3, \xi_3) = \frac{\lambda}4$.\footnote{This means that instead of $g_A(\cdot,\cdot) = -B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$, we now have $g_A(\cdot, \cdot) = -\frac18 B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$.} With this normalization, the case $A = I$ gives the round metric with sectional curvature $K = 1$ on $G \cong S^3$. \vskip 2mm We want to see which $\lambda$ in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) will arise from Sz\H{o}ke's construction. Computing at $(e,1) \in G\times S^1$, the tangent vector to the $S^1$ action we will quotient by is given by $(2\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta})$. The projection of $(\xi_3, 0)$ onto this direction is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^T & = & \frac{((\xi_3, 0), (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}))}{|\xi_3 + \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}|^2} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}), \\ & & \\ & = & \frac2{2+\mu} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}) \end{array} \end{equation} and hence the normal component is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^N & = & (\xi_3,0) - (\xi_3,0)^T \\ & & \\ & = & (\frac{\mu}{2+\mu} \xi_3, \frac2{2+\mu} \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}). \end{array} \end{equation} Thus, \[ |\xi_3^N|^2 = 2 \frac{\mu}{2+\mu}, \] which means that the quotient metric on $G$ is $g_A$ with $A$ in (\ref{eqn:A}) having $\lambda = \frac{\mu}{2 + \mu}.$ Hence, any $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ appears. The limit case $\mu = +\infty$ is just the case of the round sphere, $\lambda = 1$, which also has an entire tube, of course.
nodes.statement_short: Realise $g_\lambda$ as a Riemannian submersion quotient of $G\times S^1$ with $g_I\oplus\mu\,d\theta^2$ and apply Szőke's theorem. Projection computation gives $\lambda=\mu/(2+\mu)$, covering $(0,1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.3
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vskip 2mm \begin{enumerate} \item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right). \end{equation}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$. \end{enumerate}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition. \vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}): \[ \begin{array}{rcl} f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\mathbb{H} & = & b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, \end{array} \] where $a, b, c ,d \in \mathbb{R}$. (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\mathbb{H}'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array} \] \vskip 2mm and \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array} \] \vskip 2mm Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right). \end{equation} \vskip 2mm As to step (3), as in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly: \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} \eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\ &&&&\\ \eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3. \end{array} \] \vskip 2mm so that we have \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\ & = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). \end{array} \] \vskip 2mm It follows directly that \vskip 2mm \[ Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right). \] \vskip 2mm Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t. \end{equation} \vskip 2mm It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
nodes.statement_short: Via the rank lemma, solve the Jacobi equation along $\exp t\xi_1$, change to the right-invariant frame and reduce singularity to $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$, which has a unique positive root.

nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vskip 2mm \begin{enumerate} \item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right). \end{equation}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm \item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Recipe: reduce singularity of $D\Phi$ to a determinant $\Delta(t)$ via Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Step 1: solve the Jacobi equation
nodes.statement: Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.
nodes.statement_short: Step 1: solve the Jacobi equation

nodes.name: Step 2: fix initial conditions
nodes.statement: Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Step 2: fix initial conditions

nodes.name: Step 3: change to the right-invariant frame
nodes.statement: Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$
nodes.statement_short: Step 3: change to the right-invariant frame

nodes.name: Step 4: evaluate and solve $\Delta(t)=0$
nodes.statement: Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Step 4: evaluate and solve $\Delta(t)=0$

nodes.name: Goal: unique root $t_*(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: unique root $t_*(\lambda)$

nodes.name: Import the general Jacobi field solution
nodes.statement: Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}): \[ \begin{array}{rcl} f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\mathbb{H} & = & b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, \end{array} \] where $a, b, c ,d \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Import the general Jacobi field solution

nodes.name: Initial conditions give the Jacobi fields (5.6)
nodes.statement: (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\mathbb{H}'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array} \] \vskip 2mm and \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array} \] \vskip 2mm Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Initial conditions give the Jacobi fields (5.6)

nodes.name: Change of basis via $Ad(\exp(-t\xi_1))$
nodes.statement: As to step (3), as in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly: \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} \eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\ &&&&\\ \eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3. \end{array} \] \vskip 2mm so that we have \vskip 2mm \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\ & = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Change of basis via $Ad(\exp(-t\xi_1))$

nodes.name: Imaginary part at $it$ is diagonal
nodes.statement: It follows directly that \vskip 2mm \[ Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary part at $it$ is diagonal

nodes.name: Reduce to $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$
nodes.statement: Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if \vskip 2mm \begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t. \end{equation} \vskip 2mm It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$; unique positive root

nodes.name: Initial conditions for $Y_2, Y_3$
nodes.statement: \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right).
nodes.label: eqn:Yinit

nodes.name: Jacobi fields $f_i, h_i$
nodes.statement: \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right).
nodes.label: eqn:fhsols

nodes.name: Focal time equation $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$
nodes.statement: \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t.
nodes.label: eqn:tstar

nodes.statement: Can one carry out such a study as here for groups other than $SU(2)$?

nodes.name: Exact finite radius of Berger tubes for $\lambda>1$
nodes.statement: It may also be possible to determine the finite radius of the tubes for $\lambda \in (1,+\infty)$ using the explicit solution for the tangent vector along a geodesic for such geometries, as in section \ref{sec:U2cases} above.

nodes.name: Tube radius estimates via Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick versus Lempert-Szőke
nodes.statement: One might also find an estimate for the tube radius using an approximation to the constant negative curvature metrics on the affine elliptic curves given by the complex integrals of motion and the Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick inequality. It is unclear how such bounds would compare to the Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke curvature bound when both bounds apply.

nodes.name: Non-normal homogeneous spaces $G/H$
nodes.statement: Finally, can anything interesting be said of the case of a compact Riemannian homogeneous space $G/H$ which is not normal, i.e., not the Riemannian quotient of a symmetric metric on $G$?

nodes.name: Gelfand-Cetlin integrable systems on flag manifolds
nodes.statement: A related question would be whether Gelfand-Cetlin quantum integrable systems exist on flag manifolds, which contain the Laplacian for a non-normal homogeneous metric.

nodes.name: Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$
nodes.statement: In general, if $\gamma$ is a Riemannian geodesic with $\dot{\gamma} := T$, so that $\nabla_T T = 0$, the Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$ associates to a vectorfield $Y$ along $\gamma$ and normal to $\gamma$ the normal field along $\gamma$ given by \[ \mathcal{J}(Y) := \nabla_T^2 Y + Riem(Y, T) T. \]
